title: Patient Counseling in Massachusetts: the Offer, the Counseling and the Record
topic: Patient care / Patient counseling under 247 CMR 9.18 and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A
subtopic: When counseling is owed and to whom, who may make the offer and who may deliver the counseling, the face-to-face and telephone offer methods and the off-site toll-free pathway, the designated consultation area and the counseling rights sign, counseling availability and the measuring device, and the refusal record together with the presumption that arises from its absence
learning_objectives: Separate the three Massachusetts counseling duties — the offer, the counseling itself and the record — and name the actor, the trigger and the consequence attached to each.

State the three different triggers that operate in this area: 247 CMR 9.18(1) on each person who receives a prescription medication, M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A on any person who presents a new prescription for filling, and 247 CMR 9.18(4) on each new drug therapy and each therapy significant for the patient's health and safety.
Apply the statutory offer methods in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A and confine the alternative-method exception to the ground the statute gives it.
Distinguish who may extend the offer from who may deliver the counseling under 247 CMR 9.18(1) through (3), and place a pharmacy intern and a pharmacy technician correctly.
Work 247 CMR 9.18(5) as a professional-judgment menu of what counseling may include rather than as a mandatory script.
Apply the off-site delivery pathway in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A and state exactly where the toll-free service number must appear.

Test a consultation area against both the privacy condition and the access-route condition in 247 CMR 9.18(6), and a rights sign against the dimensions, letter height, placement and fixed wording in 247 CMR 9.18(7).
State the counseling-availability duty and the measuring-device duty in 247 CMR 9.18(8) and (9) without narrowing either one.
Apply the presumption that arises from the absence of a record of a failure to accept the offer, and say where that record may be kept.
Place the two inpatient carve-outs correctly and keep drug utilization review and the patient profile outside a counseling answer.

orientation.text: Massachusetts imposes three separate counseling duties, and almost every question in this area is decided by keeping them apart. The first is the offer. Under 247 CMR 9.18(1) a pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee shall offer the counseling services of the pharmacist to each person who receives a prescription medication, and under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A a pharmacist shall offer to counsel any person who presents a new prescription for filling. The second is the counseling itself, which under 247 CMR 9.18(3) shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern, and which 247 CMR 9.18(4) requires on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed to be significant for the health and safety of the patient. The third is the record, which M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A places on the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and which carries an evidentiary consequence when it is silent. Three duties, three actors, three triggers; a fact pattern that satisfies one of them says nothing about the other two.

The offer is the widest of the three duties and the only one a person other than a pharmacist may perform. 247 CMR 9.18(1) lets a pharmacist's designee extend it, and 247 CMR 9.18(2) supplies the control on that delegation: a pharmacist shall ensure his or her designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel. The regulation therefore constrains the designee through a training duty owed by the pharmacist rather than through a credential, which is why front-counter staff may make the offer and why no Board approval or licence class is the thing being tested. How the offer is made is fixed by statute rather than left to the pharmacy's convenience. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that the offer shall be made either by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, or by telephone, except when the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method of counseling. The two named methods are the rule and the alternative is a needs-driven exception, so a line printed on a receipt inviting the patient to ask for the pharmacist is not the statutory offer, while an alternative method for a patient who cannot use a telephone is exactly what the exception is for.

The counseling itself is narrower in every direction. 247 CMR 9.18(3) states that counseling shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern and that a pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient, so a pharmacy intern sits inside the permitted class and a pharmacy technician sits outside it however experienced or certified. The trigger in 247 CMR 9.18(4) has two limbs, and candidates lose the question by stopping at the first: counseling is required on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed to be significant for the health and safety of the patient. Refill status therefore does not end the inquiry. What the counseling contains is then governed by 247 CMR 9.18(5), which requires the pharmacist or pharmacy intern to provide such information as, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, is necessary for the patient to understand the proper use of the patient's prescription, and lists what that information may include: name, description and indication of the medication; dosage form, dosage, route of administration and duration of therapy; special directions and instructions for preparation, administration and use by the patient; common side and adverse effects or interactions and therapeutic contraindications or precautions with legend and non-legend medications and other substances the pharmacist deems relevant; techniques for self-monitoring drug therapy; proper storage and disposal; prescription refill information; and action to be taken in the event of a missed dose or adverse reaction. It is a professional-judgment menu, not a script, and it is clinical throughout.

Three of the duties in 247 CMR 9.18 are things the pharmacy must have rather than things a pharmacist must say, and they are graded on the premises. 247 CMR 9.18(6) requires a designated patient consultation area, with signage stating Patient Consultation Area, designed to provide adequate privacy for confidential visual and auditory patient counseling, and then adds a second condition that a compliant-looking room can still fail: the private consultation area shall be accessible by a patient from the outside of the prescription dispensing area without having to traverse a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area. Privacy, signage wording and the access route are three separate tests of one space. 247 CMR 9.18(7) is prescriptive in a different way. It requires a sign of not less than 11 inches in height by 14 inches in width, in a conspicuous place adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed, for the purpose of informing customers of their right to counseling by a pharmacist, in letters not less than one half inch in height, reading: Dear patients, you have the right to know about the proper use of your medication and its effects. If you need more information please ask the pharmacist. Adjacent to each dispensing area means two dispensing windows are two signs, and the size, the letter height, the placement and the wording are all separately prescribed.

Two further operational duties sit beside them and are routinely read too narrowly. Under 247 CMR 9.18(8) a pharmacy and pharmacist shall ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business, so counseling availability tracks the pharmacy's own opening rather than the presence of any particular staff arrangement. Under 247 CMR 9.18(9) a pharmacy and pharmacist shall dispense or recommend a proper measuring device with all liquid medications, and the provision carries no paediatric qualifier, no prescription-only qualifier and no controlled-substance qualifier: all liquid medications means all of them, and the duty is satisfied either by dispensing the device or by recommending one. Both duties are addressed to the pharmacy and the pharmacist together, which is worth noticing in a fact pattern that tries to locate the failure in one or the other.

Delivery away from the pharmacy has its own pathway, and it is the one place in this area where the requirements are satisfied by a piece of infrastructure rather than by a conversation. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that if a person elects delivery of a prescription drug at a location other than a pharmacy, the requirements of the section may be satisfied by providing that person with access to a toll-free telephone service to facilitate communication between the person and the pharmacist at the pharmacy. The sentence that follows is the one that decides questions: the number of that toll-free telephone service shall be printed on a label affixed to each container of a prescription drug dispensed by a pharmacy to a patient. Each container, and a label affixed to it. A number on the outer shipping carton, on the delivery receipt the patient signs, in the enclosed paperwork or in a message sent after the package arrives is not the specified placement, and the pharmacy's ordinary local number is not the specified service. Providing the access and printing the number are two steps, and a pharmacy that does the first without the second has not completed the pathway.

The record is a separate duty with its own actor and its own evidentiary consequence. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain specified patient information generated at an individual pharmacy, and that information includes any additional comments relevant to the patient's drug use and any failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel. The statute is permissive about where the information lives: it may be recorded in the patient's manual or electronic profile, in the prescription signature log, or in any other system of records, so an answer that insists on the profile alone is too narrow. Then comes the provision that runs against the intuition candidates bring to documentation questions. The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel shall create a presumption that such counseling was provided. Silence therefore operates in the pharmacist's favour, and the statute nowhere asks for an affirmative note that counseling occurred; what it asks the pharmacy to capture is the refusal. The presumption is keyed only to the state of the refusal record, so a defect elsewhere in the section — a missing container legend, a badly placed sign — neither creates nor destroys it.

Two boundaries close the section. The first is the inpatient line, which Massachusetts draws twice and in different terms. 247 CMR 9.18(10) provides that the provisions of 247 CMR 9.18 do not apply to pharmacists while practising in an inpatient setting, unless otherwise required by law or regulation, so the carve-out is keyed to the practitioner and removes the whole section rather than merely the offer. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A draws its line by reference to the drug instead: the section does not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, except to the extent required by applicable federal regulations. The second boundary is subject matter. The prospective drug utilization review that M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A requires before a new prescription is dispensed, and the contents of the patient profile that the same statute enumerates, belong to a separate topic and are not taught here. What this section states about the general duty is the umbrella proposition in its own terms: a pharmacist must comply with the patient-counseling requirements of 247 CMR 9.18 in the settings and circumstances the regulation governs, applying any narrower setting-specific, product-specific or emergency exception before the general rule.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy trains its front-counter clerks to make the offer to counsel at pickup so the pharmacist can stay at the verification station. One afternoon a clerk makes the offer on a new prescription, the patient accepts, and the patient's only question is what to do if she misses a dose. The clerk answers it from the leaflet and hands over the bag. The pharmacist-in-charge is satisfied, on the ground that the clerk was trained exactly as the regulation requires. Is the encounter compliant?
steps: Take the offer first. 247 CMR 9.18(1) allows a pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee to offer the counseling services of the pharmacist to each person who receives a prescription medication, so the clerk was a permissible person to make the offer.

Check the control on the delegation. 247 CMR 9.18(2) requires the pharmacist to ensure the designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel, and the pharmacy has done that; the training duty is what the regulation imposes, not a credential.

Now identify what happened after the offer was accepted. Answering what to take on a missed dose is counseling content: 247 CMR 9.18(5)(h) lists action to be taken in the event of a missed dose or adverse reaction among the information counseling may include.

Apply the person limit to that act. 247 CMR 9.18(3) provides that counseling shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern, and that a pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient. The clerk is an other individual.
Note that the training in 247 CMR 9.18(2) is expressly training to make the offer to counsel; it does not extend the class of persons who may counsel under 247 CMR 9.18(3).
worked_examples.resolution: The offer was properly made and the counseling was not. Once the patient accepted, the encounter had to pass to a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern. The error the scenario invites is treating the training duty in 247 CMR 9.18(2) as an authorisation that carries the designee across the line drawn by 247 CMR 9.18(3), so that the person permitted to extend the offer is assumed to be the person permitted to answer the question.

worked_examples.scenario: A chain configures its dispensing software so that the counseling prompt fires only on prescriptions the system flags as new, and is suppressed on every refill. The compliance manager explains that the regulation attaches the duty to new drug therapy, that refills by definition are not new, and that the pharmacy still posts its rights sign so any patient who wants counseling can ask. Evaluate the policy.
steps: Read 247 CMR 9.18(4) to the end. It requires counseling on each new drug therapy AND on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed to be significant for the health and safety of the patient.
Notice that the second limb is not keyed to the newness of the prescription at all. It is keyed to the significance of the therapy, assessed by the pharmacist, so a refill can sit squarely inside it.
Recognise that a software flag cannot perform the second limb, because the limb requires the pharmacist's professional judgment about this therapy and this patient.

Test the fallback the manager offers. The rights sign in 247 CMR 9.18(7) informs customers of their right to counseling by a pharmacist; it is a posting duty of the pharmacy and it does not convert the counseling duty into one that operates only on request.

Add the availability duty. Under 247 CMR 9.18(8) a pharmacy and pharmacist shall ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business, which is a further reason the pharmacy cannot design the second limb out of its workflow.
worked_examples.resolution: The policy is defective because it implements only the first limb of 247 CMR 9.18(4). The error the scenario invites is reading new drug therapy as the whole trigger and treating refill status as an answer, when the professional-judgment limb reaches any therapy significant for the patient's health and safety whatever the fill number.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy ships prescriptions to patients who elect home delivery. Its toll-free number reaches a pharmacist at the dispensing pharmacy during opening hours, and the number is printed prominently on the outside of the shipping carton and on the delivery receipt the courier collects. The pharmacy's records contain no entry showing that a particular patient failed to accept an offer to counsel. The general manager argues that because the counseling presumption runs in the pharmacy's favour, the labeling question is academic. Assess both issues.
steps: Confirm the pathway is available. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A permits the requirements of the section to be satisfied, where a person elects delivery at a location other than a pharmacy, by access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy.
Read the placement sentence exactly. The number of that toll-free telephone service shall be printed on a label affixed to each container of a prescription drug dispensed by a pharmacy to a patient.

Compare the facts. A carton is not a container of a prescription drug and a delivery receipt is not a label affixed to one, so the pharmacy has provided the access without completing the labeling step.

Turn to the second issue separately. The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel creates a presumption that such counseling was provided, and that presumption is keyed only to the state of the refusal record.
Refuse to let one issue decide the other. The presumption is not a general finding of compliance with M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, and a labeling defect is not a record of a failure to accept.
worked_examples.resolution: The remote-delivery pathway is incomplete because the toll-free number is not on a label affixed to each container, and the presumption that counseling was provided nonetheless arises because no failure to accept is recorded. The error the scenario invites is the manager's: collapsing an operational requirement and an evidentiary presumption into a single compliance verdict, so that a favourable answer on one is taken to cure the other.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy with two dispensing windows at opposite ends of a long counter posts one 11 by 14 inch counseling rights sign, correctly worded and in half-inch letters, on the wall beside the store entrance. Its consultation room is fully enclosed, quiet, and signed Private Consultation Room, but the only door into it opens off the prescription dispensing area, so a patient is escorted behind the counter to reach it. The manager treats the room as the pharmacy's strongest compliance feature. List the defects.
steps: Start with the sign's placement. 247 CMR 9.18(7) requires the sign in a conspicuous place adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed, so two dispensing windows are two areas and one sign at the entrance does not cover either of them.

Confirm what the sign does satisfy, because a defect list has to be accurate: the dimensions of not less than 11 inches by 14 inches, the letter height of not less than one half inch and the prescribed wording are all met.

Turn to the room and separate the two conditions in 247 CMR 9.18(6). The first is a designated patient consultation area designed to provide adequate privacy for confidential visual and auditory patient counseling, which the enclosed quiet room meets.

Apply the second condition, which is about the route rather than the room. The private consultation area shall be accessible by a patient from the outside of the prescription dispensing area without having to traverse a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area, and an escort behind the counter is exactly the traverse the regulation forbids.
Check the room's signage against the regulation's own words. 247 CMR 9.18(6) calls for signage stating Patient Consultation Area, so Private Consultation Room is not the prescribed designation.
worked_examples.resolution: There are three defects: the rights sign is not posted adjacent to each dispensing area, the consultation area cannot be reached without traversing the prescription dispensing area, and its signage does not state Patient Consultation Area. The error the scenario invites is grading each feature on the impression it makes — a large correct sign, a genuinely private room — rather than on the placement, access and wording conditions that 247 CMR 9.18(6) and (7) state separately.

worked_examples.scenario: During an inspection a pharmacist is asked to show that a patient was counseled on a prescription dispensed seven months earlier. The pharmacy's records contain no note that counseling was given and no note that the patient declined it. The pharmacist assumes the worst, on the footing that a documentation question with nothing in the file must go against the pharmacy, and prepares to concede the point. Is that concession correct?
steps: Identify what M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A actually asks the pharmacy to record. The pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain patient information including any failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel.
Notice what the statute does not ask for. It does not require an affirmative entry that counseling was provided; the recordable event it names on this point is the refusal.
Apply the presumption in its own terms. The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel shall create a presumption that such counseling was provided.
Match it to the facts. There is no record of a failure to accept, so the presumption arises and it runs in the pharmacist's favour rather than against him.

Keep the scope of the presumption honest. It speaks to whether counseling was provided; it does not certify that the offer was made by a statutory method or that any other requirement of the section was met.
worked_examples.resolution: The concession is wrong. On these facts the presumption that counseling was provided arises from the silence of the refusal record. The error the scenario invites is importing the ordinary recordkeeping intuition that an undocumented act is an unperformed act, when this statute reverses it by keying the presumption to the absence of a refusal entry.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.18(3), counseling shall be made by ______ or ______, and ______ may not counsel any patient.
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacist; a pharmacy intern; a pharmacy technician or other individual.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may make the offer to counsel under 247 CMR 9.18(1), and what does 247 CMR 9.18(2) require of the pharmacist about that person?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee may make the offer to each person who receives a prescription medication, and the pharmacist shall ensure his or her designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State both limbs of the counseling trigger in 247 CMR 9.18(4).
retrieval_prompts.answer: Each new drug therapy, and each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed to be significant for the health and safety of the patient.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How must the offer to counsel be made under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, and what is the only stated departure from those methods?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Either by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, or by telephone, except when the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method of counseling.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A person elects delivery of a prescription drug at home. What may satisfy the requirements of the section, and what must be printed where?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy, with the number of that service printed on a label affixed to each container of a prescription drug dispensed by the pharmacy to a patient.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What presumption arises from the absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A presumption that such counseling was provided.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three places M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A allows the patient information, including a failure to accept the offer, to be recorded.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The patient's manual or electronic profile, the prescription signature log, or any other system of records.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Give the minimum dimensions, the minimum letter height and the required placement of the counseling rights sign.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Not less than 11 inches in height by 14 inches in width, letters not less than one half inch in height, posted in a conspicuous place adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What wording must the counseling rights sign carry?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Dear patients, you have the right to know about the proper use of your medication and its effects. If you need more information please ask the pharmacist.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Beyond privacy, what does 247 CMR 9.18(6) require of the designated patient consultation area?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Signage stating Patient Consultation Area, and accessibility by a patient from the outside of the prescription dispensing area without having to traverse a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the measuring-device duty in 247 CMR 9.18(9) applies only to liquid medications dispensed for children.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. A pharmacy and pharmacist shall dispense or recommend a proper measuring device with all liquid medications.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Whom does 247 CMR 9.18(10) exclude, how much of the section does the exclusion remove, and what brings it back?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Pharmacists while practising in an inpatient setting; the provisions of 247 CMR 9.18 as a whole rather than the offer alone; unless otherwise required by law or regulation.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When must counseling be available under 247 CMR 9.18(8)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At all times when the pharmacy is open for business, as a duty of the pharmacy and the pharmacist.

quick_review.text: A pharmacist must comply with the patient-counseling requirements of 247 CMR 9.18 in the settings and circumstances the regulation governs, and any narrower setting-specific, product-specific or emergency exception is applied before the general rule.
247 CMR 9.18(1): a pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee shall offer the counseling services of the pharmacist to each person who receives a prescription medication.

247 CMR 9.18(2): a pharmacist shall ensure his or her designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel; the control is a training duty on the pharmacist, not a credential on the designee.
247 CMR 9.18(3): counseling shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern, and a pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient.

247 CMR 9.18(4): counseling is required on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed significant for the health and safety of the patient.

247 CMR 9.18(5): the pharmacist or intern provides such information as professional judgment makes necessary for the patient to understand proper use, and the enumerated items are what counseling may include rather than a required script.

M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A: a pharmacist shall offer to counsel any person who presents a new prescription for filling, by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, or by telephone, except when the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method.

Where a person elects delivery at a location other than a pharmacy, the requirements may be satisfied by access to a toll-free telephone service that facilitates communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy.
The toll-free service number shall be printed on a label affixed to each container of a prescription drug dispensed by the pharmacy to a patient.

The pharmacist or designee shall make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain the specified patient information, which includes any additional comments relevant to the patient's drug use and any failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel.
The information may be recorded in the patient's manual or electronic profile, in the prescription signature log, or in any other system of records.
The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel creates a presumption that such counseling was provided; no affirmative counseling note is required for it to arise.

247 CMR 9.18(6): a designated patient consultation area, signed Patient Consultation Area, giving adequate privacy for confidential visual and auditory counseling, and reachable from outside the prescription dispensing area without traversing a stockroom or that area.

247 CMR 9.18(7): a sign of not less than 11 inches by 14 inches, in letters not less than one half inch high, in a conspicuous place adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed, carrying the prescribed wording about the right to counseling.

247 CMR 9.18(8) and (9): a pharmacy and pharmacist shall ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business, and shall dispense or recommend a proper measuring device with all liquid medications.
247 CMR 9.18(10): the provisions of 247 CMR 9.18 do not apply to pharmacists while practising in an inpatient setting unless otherwise required by law or regulation.

decision_logic.condition: A person is receiving a prescription medication at the pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Make the offer under 247 CMR 9.18(1). A pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee may make it, provided the pharmacist has ensured the designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription the person presents for filling is a new prescription.
decision_logic.action: The statutory offer duty in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A attaches as well. Make the offer by face to face communication or by telephone, and use an alternative method only where the patient's needs or availability require it.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is a refill and the therapy is not new.
decision_logic.action: Do not stop there. Apply the second limb of 247 CMR 9.18(4) and ask whether this drug therapy is, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, significant for the health and safety of the patient.

decision_logic.condition: Counseling is to be provided, whether because the offer was taken up or because 247 CMR 9.18(4) requires it.
decision_logic.action: Hand the encounter to a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern. A pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient, and training to make the offer does not change that.

decision_logic.condition: You are deciding what the counseling should cover.
decision_logic.action: Provide what professional judgment makes necessary for the patient to understand proper use of the prescription, drawing on the 247 CMR 9.18(5) list of clinical items rather than reciting it or adding commercial information to it.

decision_logic.condition: The person elects delivery of the prescription drug at a location other than a pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Provide access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy, and print that number on a label affixed to each container. Both steps are required; neither substitutes for the other.

decision_logic.condition: The person declines the offer to counsel.
decision_logic.action: Record the failure to accept as part of the reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain patient information; the profile, the prescription signature log or any other system of records will do.

decision_logic.condition: You are asked whether counseling was provided on a past fill and the file is silent.
decision_logic.action: Look specifically for a record of a failure to accept the offer. Its absence creates the presumption that counseling was provided, so do not concede the point for want of an affirmative note.

decision_logic.condition: You are auditing the pharmacy's premises for counseling compliance.
decision_logic.action: Test the consultation area for privacy, for the Patient Consultation Area signage and for the access route; then test the rights sign for its dimensions, letter height, conspicuous placement adjacent to each dispensing area and prescribed wording.

decision_logic.condition: A liquid medication is being dispensed, or the pharmacy is setting its opening hours and staffing.
decision_logic.action: Dispense or recommend a proper measuring device whatever the patient's age, and ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist is practising in an inpatient setting, or the drug is dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home.
decision_logic.action: Apply the carve-outs before the general rule: 247 CMR 9.18 does not apply to pharmacists practising in an inpatient setting unless otherwise required by law or regulation, and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A does not apply to such a drug except to the extent required by applicable federal regulations.

decision_logic.condition: The facts are about screening the prescription rather than about talking to the patient or recording the encounter.
decision_logic.action: Recognise that as prospective drug utilization review and the patient profile, a separate topic, and do not answer it out of 247 CMR 9.18 or out of the counseling paragraphs of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A.

ma_vs_federal.text: No federal counseling rule is among this section's dependencies, so no federal counseling standard is stated here. The only federal reference inside the declared scope is a carve-back: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A withdraws its own inpatient exclusion to the extent applicable federal regulations require otherwise.

247 CMR 9.18(10) uses a wider formula for the same idea, disapplying the section to pharmacists practising in an inpatient setting unless otherwise required by law or regulation, which reaches other law as well as federal regulation.

exceptions.text: Any narrower setting-specific, product-specific or emergency exception is applied before the general patient-counseling rule.
The statutory offer methods yield to an alternative method of counseling when, and only when, the patient's needs or availability require it.

Where a person elects delivery of a prescription drug at a location other than a pharmacy, the requirements of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A may be satisfied by access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy.

The content of counseling is not fixed: 247 CMR 9.18(5) requires such information as, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, is necessary for the patient to understand proper use, and the enumerated items are what it may include.

247 CMR 9.18 does not apply to pharmacists while practising in an inpatient setting, unless otherwise required by law or regulation, and the exclusion covers the whole section rather than the offer alone.
M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A does not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, except to the extent required by applicable federal regulations.

timing_deadlines.event: A person receives a prescription medication
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At receipt of the prescription medication
timing_deadlines.consequence: The offer of the pharmacist's counseling services is owed then, and a pharmacist or an appropriately trained designee must make it.

timing_deadlines.event: A person presents a new prescription for filling
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At presentation of the new prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: The statutory duty to offer to counsel attaches, by face to face communication or by telephone unless the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method.

timing_deadlines.event: The pharmacy is open for business
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At all times while the pharmacy is open
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy and pharmacist must ensure counseling is available throughout; there is no stretch of opening hours in which it may be unavailable.

timing_deadlines.event: A prescription drug is dispensed for delivery at a location other than a pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Before the container leaves the pharmacy
timing_deadlines.consequence: The toll-free service number must already be printed on a label affixed to that container, so a number supplied after delivery does not complete the pathway.

forms_records.text: The record that matters most in this area is the record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel, which sits inside the patient information the pharmacist or designee must make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain.
Any additional comments relevant to the patient's drug use fall inside the same body of information to be obtained, recorded and maintained.

The permitted locations are stated in the alternative: the patient's manual or electronic profile, the prescription signature log, or any other system of records. An answer confined to the patient profile is too narrow.

The statute attaches an evidentiary consequence to the state of that record rather than to its contents: absence of any record of a failure to accept creates a presumption that counseling was provided, and no affirmative note that counseling occurred is required to raise it.

On the off-site delivery route the record-bearing artefact is the container label itself, which must carry the number of the toll-free telephone service on each container of a prescription drug dispensed to the patient.

Two postings are themselves prescribed records of a kind: signage stating Patient Consultation Area at the designated consultation area, and the counseling rights sign with its prescribed size, letter height, placement and wording.
For the designee the regulation states a training duty on the pharmacist rather than a form: the pharmacist shall ensure his or her designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel.

The 247 CMR 9.18(5) list is not a checklist to be completed and filed. It describes information the pharmacist or intern may provide as professional judgment requires, so a completed form is not what demonstrates compliance with it.

The enumerated contents of the patient profile itself, and the prospective drug utilization review that precedes dispensing, are recordkeeping subjects belonging to a separate topic and are not stated here.

role_duties.duty: Comply with the patient-counseling requirements of 247 CMR 9.18 in the settings and circumstances the regulation governs, applying any narrower setting-specific, product-specific or emergency exception first.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist making or delegating the offer
role_duties.duty: Offer the counseling services of the pharmacist to each person who receives a prescription medication, and ensure that any designee who makes the offer is appropriately trained to do so.

Offer to counsel any person who presents a new prescription for filling, by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, or by telephone, unless the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern delivering counseling
role_duties.duty: Provide the counseling itself, on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy deemed significant for the patient's health and safety, giving such information as professional judgment makes necessary for the patient to understand proper use.
May extend the offer to counsel once appropriately trained by the pharmacist, and may participate in obtaining and recording the patient information, but may not deliver the counseling.
May not counsel any patient; being permitted to make the offer as a designee does not confer authority to provide the pharmacist's counseling.

Maintain a designated patient consultation area with the prescribed signage, adequate visual and auditory privacy, and an access route that does not require the patient to traverse a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area.

Post a sign of not less than 11 by 14 inches, in letters not less than one half inch high, in a conspicuous place adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed, carrying the prescribed wording about the right to counseling by a pharmacist.
Ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business, and dispense or recommend a proper measuring device with all liquid medications.

Provide access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy, and print that service number on a label affixed to each prescription-drug container dispensed to the patient.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or designee keeping the record
role_duties.duty: Make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain the specified patient information, including any failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel, in the profile, the prescription signature log or another system of records.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist practising in an inpatient setting
role_duties.duty: Is outside the provisions of 247 CMR 9.18 unless otherwise required by law or regulation, so the counseling analysis for that practice starts elsewhere.

common_traps.text: Treating the offer and the counseling as one duty, so that a trained designee's authority to extend the offer is read as authority to counsel. 247 CMR 9.18(3) bars a pharmacy technician or other individual from counseling any patient.

Stopping at the first limb of 247 CMR 9.18(4) and concluding that a refill can never require counseling, when the professional-judgment limb reaches any therapy significant for the patient's health and safety.
Treating the 247 CMR 9.18(5) list as a mandatory script, or expecting commercial information such as acquisition cost to sit inside a list that is clinical throughout.

Reading the patient's needs or availability exception in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A as making any method of offer acceptable at the pharmacy's convenience, rather than as a departure the patient's own circumstances must require.

Treating the toll-free number as satisfied by the outer shipping package, the delivery receipt, the enclosed paperwork or a message after delivery, when the statute specifies a label affixed to each container.
Assuming the counseling rights sign is a once-per-store requirement. It is required adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed.
Checking only the size of the rights sign. The minimum dimensions, the minimum letter height, the conspicuous placement and the prescribed wording are all separately stated.

Grading a consultation area on privacy alone. A fully enclosed room still fails if the patient cannot reach it without traversing a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area, or if its signage does not state Patient Consultation Area.
Narrowing the measuring-device duty to paediatric liquids, when 247 CMR 9.18(9) reaches all liquid medications and is satisfied by dispensing or by recommending a proper device.
Reading the inpatient carve-out in 247 CMR 9.18(10) as removing only the offer, when it disapplies the provisions of 247 CMR 9.18 as a whole unless otherwise required by law or regulation.

Assuming an unrecorded encounter means counseling cannot be shown, or that the presumption depends on an affirmative record that counseling occurred. It is the absence of a record of a failure to accept that raises it.
Restricting the permitted record to the patient profile, when the prescription signature log and any other system of records are equally available.

Letting a defect in one duty decide another: a labeling failure on the off-site route neither creates nor destroys the record-based presumption, and the presumption is not a general certificate of compliance.

Substituting a general meaningful-offer formula for the terms Massachusetts actually uses. The regulation requires the offer of the pharmacist's counseling services to each person who receives a prescription medication, and the statute fixes the methods by which the offer is made.
Answering a counseling question out of the prospective drug utilization review or the patient profile requirements, which are a separate topic with their own trigger.
